source_text: Τῶν πρώην ἡμῖν εἰς ἐξέτασιν προτεθέντων λόγων καὶ τὴν ἀνάστασιν πιστουμένων πάντες μέν εἰσιν ὁμογενεῖς, ὡς ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς φύντες ἀρχῆς· ἀρχὴ γὰρ αὐτοῖς ἡ τῶν πρώτων ἀνθρώπων ἐκ δημιουργίας γένεσις· ἀλλ᾿ οἱ μὲν ἐξ αὐτῆς κρατύνονται τῆς πρώτης ἀρχῆς ἐξ ἧσπερ ἔφυσαν, οἱ δέ, παρεπόμενοι τῇ τε φύσει καὶ τῷ βίῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἐκ τῆς τοῦ θεοῦ περὶ ἡμᾶς προνοίας λαμβάνουσι τὴν πίστιν· ἡ μὲν γὰρ αἰτία, καθ᾿ ἣν καὶ δι᾿ ἣν γεγόνασιν ἄνθρωποι, συνεζευγμένη τῇ φύσει τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ἐκ δημιουργίας ἔχει τὴν ἰσχύν, ὁ δὲ τῆς δικαιοσύνης λόγος, καθ᾿ ὃν κρίνει θεὸς τοὺς εὖ ἢ κακῶς βεβιωκότας ἀνθρώπους, ἐκ τοῦ τούτων τέλους· φύονται μὲν γὰρ ἐκεῖθεν, ἤρτηνται δὲ μᾶλλον τῆς προνοίας. Δεδειγμένων δὲ ἡμῖν τῶν πρώτων ὡς οἷόν τε, καλῶς ἂν ἔχοι καὶ διὰ τῶν ὑστέρων δεῖξαι τὸ προκείμενον, λέγω δὲ διὰ τῆς ὀφειλομένης ἑκάστῳ τῶν ἀνθρώπων κατὰ δικαίαν κρίσιν τιμῆς ἢ δίκης καὶ τοῦ κατὰ τὸν ἀνθρώπινον βίον τέλους, αὐτῶν δὲ τούτων προτάξαι τὸν κατὰ φύσιν ἡγούμενον, καὶ πρῶτόν γε διασκέψασθαι τὸν περὶ τῆς κρίσεως λόγον· τοσοῦτον μόνον ὑπειπόντας, φροντίδι τῆς προσηκούσης τοῖς προκειμένοις ἀρχῆς καὶ τάξεως, ὅτι δεῖ τοὺς ποιητὴν τὸν θεὸν τοῦδε τοῦ παντὸς παραδεξαμένους τῇ τούτου σοφίᾳ καὶ δικαιοσύνῃ τὴν τῶν γενομένων ἁπάντων ἀνατιθέναι φυλακήν τε καὶ πρόνοιαν, εἴ γε ταῖς ἰδίαις ἀρχαῖς παραμένειν ἐθέλοιεν, ταῦτα δὲ περὶ τούτων φρονοῦντας μηδὲν ἡγεῖσθαι μήτε τῶν κατὰ γῆν μήτε τῶν κατ᾿ οὐρανὸν ἀνεπιτρόπευτον μηδ᾿ ἀπρονόητον, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπὶ πᾶν ἀφανὲς ὀμοίως καὶ φαινόμενον, μικρόν τε καὶ μεῖζον, διήκουσαν γινώσκειν τὴν παρὰ τοῦ ποιήσαντος ἐπιμέλειαν. Δεῖται γὰρ πάντα τὰ γενόμενα τῆς παρὰ τοῦ ποιήσαντος ἐπιμελείας, ἰδίως δὲ ἕκαστον καθ᾿ ὃ πέφυκε καὶ πρὸς ὃ πέφυκεν· ἀχρείου γὰρ οἶμαι φιλοτιμίας τὸ κατάγειν ἢ διαιρεῖν νῦν ἢ τὸ πρόσφορον ἑκάστῃ φύσει καταλέγειν ἐθέλειν. Ὅ γε μὴν ἄνθρωπος, περὶ οὗ νῦν πρόκειται λέγειν, ὡς μὲν ἐνδεὴς δεῖται τροφῆς, ὡς δὲ θνητὸς διαδοχῆς, ὡς δὲ λογικὸς δίκης. Εἰ δὲ τῶν εἰρημένων ἕκαστόν ἐστιν ἀνθρώπῳ κατὰ φύσιν, καὶ δεῖται μὲν τροφῆς διὰ τὴν ζωήν, δεῖται δὲ διαδοχῆς διὰ τὴν τοῦ γένους διαμονήν, δεῖται δὲ δίκης διὰ τὸ τῆς τροφῆς καὶ τῆς διαδοχῆς ἔννομον, ἀνάγκη δήπου, τῆς τροφῆς καὶ τῆς διαδοχῆς ἐπὶ τὸ συναμφότερον φερομένης, ἐπὶ τοῦτο φέρεσθαι καὶ τὴν δίκην, λέγω δὲ συναμφότερον τὸν ἐκ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος ἄνθρωπον, καὶ τὸν τοιοῦτον ἄνθρωπον γίνεσθαι πάντων τῶν πεπραγμένων ὑπόδικον, τήν τε ἐπὶ τούτοις δέχεσθαι τιμὴν ἢ τιμωρίαν. Εἰ δὲ κατὰ τοῦ συναμφοτέρου φέρει τὴν ἐπὶ τοῖς εἰργασμένοις δίκην ἡ δικαία κρίσις, καὶ μήτε τὴν ψυχὴν μόνην δεῖ κομίσασθαι τὰ ἐπίχειρα τῶν μετὰ τοῦ σώματος εἰργασμένων (ἀπροσπαθὴς γὰρ αὕτη καθ᾿ ἑαυτὴν τῶν περὶ τὰς σωματικὰς ἡδονὰς ἢ τροφὰς καὶ θεραπείας γινομένων πλημμελημάτων) μήτε τὸ σῶμα μόνον (ἄκριτον γὰρ τοῦτο καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸ νόμου καὶ δίκης), ὁ δὲ ἐκ τούτων ἄνθρωπος τὴν ἐφ᾿ ἑκάστῳ τῶν εἰργασμένων αὐτῷ δέχεται κρίσιν, τοῦτο δὲ οὔτε κατὰ τήνδε τὴν ζωὴν εὑρίσκει συμβαῖνον ὁ λόγος (οὐ γὰρ σώζεται τὸ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν ἐν τῷ παρόντι βίῳ, διὰ τὸ πολλοὺς μὲν ἀθέους καὶ πᾶσαν ἀνομίαν καὶ κακίαν ἐπιτηδεύοντας μέχρι τελευτῆς διατελεῖν κακῶν ἀπειράτους, καὶ τοὐναντίον τοὺς κατὰ πᾶσαν ἀρετὴν ἐξητασμένον τὸν ἑαυτῶν βίον ἐπιδειξαμένους ἐν ὀδύναις ζῆν, ἐν ἐπηρείαις, ἐν συκοφαντίαις, αἰκίαις τε καὶ παντοίαις κακοπαθείαις) οὔτε δὲ μετὰ θάνατον (οὐδὲ γὰρ ἔστιν ἔτι τὸ συναμφότερον, χωριζομένης μὲν τῆς ψυχῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ σώματος, σκεδαννυμένου δὲ καὶ αὐτοῦ τοῦ σώματος εἰς ἐκεῖνα πάλιν ἐξ ὦν συνεφορήθη, καὶ μηδὲν ἔτι σώζοντος τῆς προτέρας φυῆς ἢ μορφῆς, ἤ πού γε τὴν μνήμην τῶν πεπραγμένων), εὔδηλον παντὶ τὸ λειπόμενον, ὅτι δεῖ κατὰ τὸν ἀπόστολον τὸ φθαρτὸν τοῦτο καὶ σκεδαστὸν ἐνδύσασθαι ἀφθαρσίαν, ἵνα, ζωοποιηθέντων ἐξ ἀναστάσεως τῶν νεκρωθέντων καὶ πάλιν ἑνωθέντων τῶν κεχωρισμένων ἢ καὶ πάντη διαλελυμένων, ἕκαστος κομίσηται δικαίως ἃ διὰ τοῦ σώματος ἔπραξεν, εἴτε ἀγαθὰ εἴτε κακά.
pass_a_gloss: Of the words previously proposed to us for examination and the resurrection being believed by all, they are all of the same kind, as having sprung from the same origin; for their origin is the genesis of the first humans from creation; but some are strong in the first origin from which they sprang, others, following both the nature and the life of humans, receive faith from the forethought of God concerning us; for the cause by which and through which humans have come to be, being yoked to human nature, has its power from creation, but the word of righteousness, by which God judges humans who have lived well or badly, is from their end; for they spring from there, but are more dependent on forethought. Having shown the first as well as possible, it would be good to show the proposed thing also through the later ones, I mean through the reward or punishment owed to each human according to just judgment and the end according to human life, and to propose first the one leading according to nature, and to examine first the word concerning judgment; assuming only this, with the care of the befitting beginning and order, that one must assign to God the creator of this universe the guardianship and forethought of all things that have come to be, if they wish to remain in their own beginnings, and considering these things, they think nothing is unmanaged or unprovided for, either on earth or in heaven, but the care from the one who made them extends to all things, visible and invisible, small and great. For all things that have come to be need the care from the one who made them, especially each one according to what it has been made and for what it has been made; for I think it is unnecessary to bring down or divide now or to wish to assign what is suitable to each nature. But the human, concerning whom it is now proposed to speak, as being in need, needs nourishment, as being mortal, needs succession, as being rational, needs judgment. If each of the things mentioned is according to nature for humans, and they need nourishment for life, and need succession for the preservation of the genus, and need judgment for the lawful use of nourishment and succession, it is necessary, therefore, that judgment also be brought to the same thing to which nourishment and succession are brought, I mean to the human being composed of soul and body, and that such a human becomes subject to judgment for all things done, and receives reward or punishment for these things. If just judgment brings judgment for the things done to the whole human, and neither the soul alone should bear the consequences of the things done with the body (for it is not responsible by itself for the faults concerning bodily pleasures or nourishments and treatments), nor the body alone (for it is not capable of law and judgment by itself), but the human composed of these receives judgment for each of the things done, this is not found to happen in this life (for the worthy things are not saved in the present life, because many atheists and those practicing all lawlessness and wickedness continue until death, and on the other hand, those who have examined their life according to all virtue live in pains, in plots, in slanders, in injustices, and all kinds of sufferings), nor after death (for the whole human no longer exists, with the soul being separated from the body, and the body itself being dissolved again into the things from which it was composed, and nothing of the former nature or form being preserved, nor even the memory of the things done), it is clear to everyone what is lacking, that the perishable and dissolvable thing must put on imperishability, so that, when the dead are made alive through resurrection and the separated or completely dissolved things are reunited, each one may justly bear the consequences of what they did through the body, whether good or bad.

pass_b_english: All the statements previously set before us for examination, which also attest the resurrection, share the same kind: they spring from the same origin, since their origin is the creation of the first humans. Some hold fast to that first origin from which they arose; others, following the nature and life of human beings, receive faith from God's providence toward us. The cause by which and through which humans came to be is yoked to human nature and draws its power from creation, but the word of righteousness by which God judges those who have lived well or badly derives from their end; they spring from that end, yet depend more on providence.

Having shown the first points as fully as possible, it would be good to demonstrate the proposed thesis also through the later ones — I mean through the honor or penalty owed to each person according to just judgment and the end appropriate to human life — and to set forth first the principle that leads according to nature, and to examine first the account concerning judgment. We assume only this, with due care for the proper beginning and order: we must assign to God the creator of this universe the guardianship and providence over all things that have come to be, if we wish to remain true to our own first principles. Holding this view, we consider nothing — whether on earth or in heaven, visible or invisible, small or great — to be unmanaged or without providence; rather, the care of the Maker extends to all alike. For everything that has come to be needs the care of its Maker, each according to what it is and for what it was made. I think it would be pointless now to lower or divide things, or to try to assign what suits each nature.

Man, about whom we now speak, as one who is in need requires nourishment; as mortal he requires succession; as rational he requires judgment. If each of these is natural to man, and he needs nourishment for life, succession for the continuation of the race, and judgment for the lawful use of nourishment and succession, then judgment must also be brought to the same whole to which nourishment and succession are brought — I mean the human being composed of soul and body — and such a human becomes accountable for all that is done, receiving honor or punishment accordingly. If just judgment renders judgment upon the whole person for what was done, then neither the soul alone should bear the consequences of deeds done with the body (for by itself it is not responsible for failings concerning bodily pleasures, nourishment, and care), nor the body alone (for by itself it lacks capacity for law and judgment), but the human being composed of these receives judgment for each deed. Yet this is not found to happen in this life (for worth is not rewarded in the present life, since many atheists practicing all lawlessness and wickedness continue to the end without suffering evil, while those who have ordered their lives by every virtue live in pains, plots, slanders, injustices, and all kinds of afflictions), nor after death (for the whole person no longer exists: the soul is separated from the body, the body itself dissolves back into the elements from which it was composed, and nothing of the former nature or form remains, nor even the memory of deeds done). It is therefore clear to everyone what is lacking: as the apostle says, this perishable and dissoluble body must put on imperishability (1 Corinthians 15:53-54), so that when the dead are made alive through resurrection and the separated or completely dissolved parts are reunited, each may justly receive the consequences of what he did through the body, whether good or bad.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the unity of soul and body and the necessity of resurrection for just judgment. Pass A preserves all clauses and nuances of the Greek. Pass B provides a fluent rendering that remains faithful to the Greek and Pass A. The scripture citation (1 Corinthians 15:53-54) is correctly identified as the source for the allusion to the apostle's words regarding the perishable putting on imperishability.
